title: Program structure, blocks and comments
summary: SLANG is free-format and requires MAIN(). Prefer { ... } for new function bodies. Brackets, Japanese corner brackets, and legacy BEGIN ... END; blocks remain accepted; parentheses delimit function argument lists, not blocks.
notes: Keep an array name attached to its opening bracket: T [1] is not read as an element access. The original specification also forbids whitespace between a function name and its opening parenthesis; slangc accepts a space there, but write NAME( so the source stays portable.
Strings and // comments cannot continue onto the next source line. Block comments do not nest.
MAIN() may appear anywhere but must be defined. slangc does not report a missing MAIN; the generated startup code calls MAIN, so the output then fails to assemble.

title: BYTE, WORD, FLOAT, VAR, ARRAY and CONST
summary: WORD is the default 16-bit type, BYTE is 8-bit, and slangc adds a 24-bit FLOAT. VAR declares variables, ARRAY allocates indexed storage, and CONST defines compile-time values, either globally or among the declarations of a function.
syntax: VAR A, BYTE B, FLOAT F;
MAIN() { CONST K=7; VAR A; A=K; }
notes: ARRAY T NAME[n] allocates indexes 0 through n, so it contains n+1 elements. Missing initial values are filled with 0; too many values is an error.
BYTE uses 1 byte in static storage. Local BYTE and WORD values occupy 2-byte argument/local slots; FLOAT occupies 3 bytes.
Integer values convert to FLOAT automatically. Convert FLOAT to an integer explicitly with FTOI.
A VAR declared with [] is indirect: its value is treated as the base address for indexed memory access.

Initial values of global and static variables must be integer constants known at that point: literals, CONST names and expressions of them. An expression that uses a variable or label address (VAR X = &Y) or a FLOAT is an error. A global FLOAT variable may start from a FLOAT literal, a FLOAT CONST or a constant expression that folds to one value.

CONST may be declared inside a function, among its declarations before the first statement. The value must be an integer or FLOAT constant known at that point. A function-local CONST cannot be used before its declaration, cannot be assigned, incremented, taken with & or indexed, cannot be used in #IF, and cannot reuse the name of a global function, VAR, ARRAY, CONST or MACHINE (that is the error CONST 'K' in function 'MAIN' has the same name as a global name), a parameter or another local of the same function.

CONST ASM NAME=value; is global only. Besides defining the constant it writes NAME EQU value into the generated assembly, so #ASM blocks and library code can refer to it; a library parameter guarded by #IF can be overridden by a CONST ASM placed before the #INCLUDE.
TRUE (1) and FALSE (0) are predefined. They cannot be used as variable, array or parameter names.

examples.title: Global and function-local constants

title: Functions, arguments and return types
summary: Functions can declare BYTE, WORD or FLOAT parameters and return types. WORD is the default; FLOAT functions return a 24-bit value and require explicit FTOI conversion when consumed as an integer.
notes: slangc checks the argument count of every call to a user-defined function, with or without parameter types: a mismatch is the error Function 'NAME' expects n arguments, got m. An integer argument for a FLOAT parameter is converted; a FLOAT argument for a WORD or BYTE parameter is an error.
WORD return values use HL; FLOAT return values use AHL.
Declarations before a function block are static. Declarations inside the block are dynamic locals, limited to 240 bytes per function.

The caller writes the arguments from (IY+$70) upward, so a function's parameters may take at most 16 bytes together (BYTE, WORD and arrays 2 bytes, FLOAT 3 bytes); a longer parameter list is an error.

A parameter, local or static variable with the same name as a global CONST is that variable inside the function; the CONST value is not folded in. Such a name cannot be used in the function's declaration expressions (array sizes, addresses, initial values).

A function whose name the assembler cannot use as a label (a Z80 instruction, register or condition name such as ADD, F, H or NZ, EQU, or a name that reads as a hexadecimal number such as ABH) gets the entry label _F_<name>, for example _F_ADD. Use that label when calling it from #ASM.

examples.title: A parameter named like a global CONST is the parameter

title: MACHINE declarations and calling convention
summary: MACHINE binds a SLANG function name to an external Z80 routine. The declared argument count controls whether values are passed in registers or on the stack, and every call must pass exactly that many arguments.
notes: Use an explicit argument count. 0 arguments: CALL only. 1: HL. 2: HL then DE. 3: HL, DE and BC. For 4 or more, every WORD argument is pushed on the stack left-to-right and the caller removes 2 bytes per argument after return.

A call that passes a different number of arguments than the declaration is an error (Function 'P' expects 2 arguments, got 1). The built-in functions BEEP, STOP, LOCATE, INKEY, INPUT, GETL, GETLIN, LINPUT, WIDTH, SCREEN, PRMODE, BIT, SET, RESET, ABS, SEX, SGN, RND, VTOS, GETREG and CALL are MACHINE functions with fixed counts and are checked the same way.

The historical omitted count (arguments on the stack and their number in HL) is not supported. MACHINE NAME(); and MACHINE NAME:address; declare a routine with 0 arguments, and passing any argument to it is an error.

Other runtime functions, such as VSYNC, STICK, TATTR, PCGDEF, FOPEN or the PSG calls, are not declared to the compiler: slangc passes the call's arguments in the same registers and does not check how many there are, so follow each function's documented argument count. Only the runtime functions with typed arguments (the FLOAT functions, FTOI, ITOF and UTOF) have their argument count checked. A MACHINE declaration with the same name as a runtime function replaces that function's call contract.

A FLOAT value can be passed to a MACHINE function only as its single argument when the declaration also has one argument; it arrives in AHL. MACHINE functions return WORD only; a FLOAT return annotation is rejected.

title: Inline Z80 assembly with MACHINE and #ASM
aliases: インラインアセンブラ
summary: Declare an explicit-arity MACHINE function and place its Z80 target in a #ASM ... #END block to call inline assembly from SLANG.
notes: A numeric MACHINE target calls that absolute address. A symbolic target is resolved in the combined compiler output, so it may name a label in a later #ASM block.
Explicit counts 0 through 3 pass WORD arguments in no registers, HL, HL then DE, or HL then DE then BC. A WORD result is returned in HL; AF, BC, DE, HL and IX are caller-clobbered.

For an explicit count of 4 or more, all WORD arguments are pushed left-to-right. At entry to a four-argument callee, after the CALL return address, argument 4 is at SP+2, argument 3 at SP+4, argument 2 at SP+6 and argument 1 at SP+8. After the call returns its WORD in HL, the caller exchanges HL with DE, adjusts SP by 2 bytes per argument through HL, then exchanges DE back into HL; the result is therefore restored to HL after cleanup.

IX is not a preserved compiler work pointer and may be clobbered; IY must be preserved because the generated program uses it as its work pointer. Restore SP so RET consumes the original return address, restore any alternate registers you touch, return in the normal register bank, and leave interrupt-enable state unchanged. Alternate registers are not a supported argument or result channel.

Always write the explicit argument count. MACHINE NAME():label declares a routine with 0 arguments, and passing any argument to it is an error; calls with a count different from the declaration are rejected.
To call a SLANG function from #ASM, use its entry label: normally the function name, or _F_<name> when the name is a Z80 instruction, register or condition name or reads as a hexadecimal number.

A runtime routine called from #ASM is put into the program only when it is called with an upper-case CALL NAME line inside a function's #ASM. A CALL in a top-level #ASM (outside any function) does not bring it in, and the program fails to assemble unless something else did. Ask for it with a line ; @calls NAME (names separated by commas, at the start of a line) inside that top-level #ASM; the bundled TILELIB.LIB and CHIPLIB.LIB ask for MULHLDE this way. A name that is not a runtime routine of the environment is ignored with a warning; a name that is also one of the program's own functions is an error, so a program that includes those libraries cannot have a function named MULHLDE. ; @calls lines in a function's #ASM are only comments.

examples.title: Call an inline routine that prints 223

title: IF, loops, CASE, EXIT and CONTINUE
summary: SLANG supports structured conditionals and loops, CASE selection, EXIT, multi-level EXIT(n), EXIT TO and CONTINUE.
syntax: EXIT;  EXIT(n);  EXIT TO label;  CONTINUE;
notes: FOR is do-while-like: its body executes before the end value is tested. A range that already passed its end can still execute once.
CASE tests clauses from top to bottom and exits after the first match. Clauses may contain a value, a range with TO, or comma-separated values.
ELSE IF may also be written ELSEIF or EF.

EXIT leaves the innermost loop and EXIT(n) leaves n enclosing loops at once; EXIT is the same as EXIT(1). n must be a constant from 1 up to the number of enclosing loops; a variable, 0 or too large a level is an error, and so is EXIT outside a loop.
CASE is not a loop: EXIT and CONTINUE inside a CASE act on the loop around it, and EXIT(n) does not count the CASE.

CONTINUE goes on to the next round of the innermost loop: for FOR, to the step of the control variable; for WHILE, to the condition; for REPEAT, to the UNTIL condition; for LOOP, to the top of the body. CONTINUE outside a loop is an error.
A FLOAT value cannot be a condition of IF, WHILE, UNTIL or ?:, nor an operand of &&, || or NOT; slangc reports A FLOAT value cannot be used as a condition. Compare it instead: IF F <> 0.0 THEN ...

examples.title: Leave two nested loops with EXIT(2)

title: Operators and signed arithmetic
summary: Integer arithmetic is 16-bit, and ordinary operators are unsigned where it matters. Dot operators provide signed multiply, divide, shifts and comparisons; slangc also supports logical &&/||, prefix and postfix ++/--, compound assignments and ?:.
notes: AND, OR and XOR have lower precedence than comparison operators in the historical precedence table; use parentheses for clarity.
Relation results use TRUE=1 and FALSE=0, also when the operands are FLOAT.
The ampersand address operator returns the address of a variable or array element.
Shift counts use only their low 4 bits, for <<, >>, .<<. and .>>.: a count of 16 shifts by 0 and 17 by 1, so 1 << 16 is 1 and $8000 >> 16 is $8000. >> is unsigned (zeros enter from the left).

Constant expressions are folded to the value the program would compute at run time. CONST A = 1 << 16; makes A equal to 1. /, MOD and >> cut a negative constant to 16 bits and work unsigned, so -7 / 2 is $7FFC and -2 >> 1 is $7FFF.

Postfix ++ and -- give the value before the change and prefix ++ and -- the value after it, also for array elements, indirect variables and MEM[]: with A=1, B = A++ + 10; sets B to 11 and A to 2. Using the value of a postfix ++/-- on a FLOAT is an error; use the prefix form or a separate statement.

The value of an assignment (=, += and the others) is the value written, converted to the target's type. The order of side effects (assignments, ++, function calls) relative to other reads in the same expression is not defined.

Only variables, array elements, MEM[], MEMW[], SOS[], SOSW[], PORT[], PORTW[] and indirect-variable elements can be assigned. ++, -- and the compound assignments compute the target's address twice, once to read and once to write, so a side effect in the target's index (T[I++] += 1, T[I++]++) is an error, as is a compound right-hand side that assigns a variable the target's index reads (T[I] += (I = I + 1)).

examples.title: Postfix increment value and 16-bit shift counts

title: Preprocessor, includes and environment constants
summary: Use #INCLUDE for the bundled libraries and #IF for environment-dependent code. X1Pen compiles in slangc's x1 environment, where ENV_TYPE=1 and OS_TYPE=0 (LSX-Dodgers on the X1).
notes: slangc reads an #INCLUDE file each time it is named, also when another included file already read it. A file that makes labels (a function, an ARRAY, a CONST holding a machine-code table, a CONST ASM, which becomes an EQU, or a label inside an #ASM block) then makes them twice, and the program fails to assemble with Duplicate label errors; a file of plain CONST values, MACHINE declarations or statements only can be read twice. All eight bundled libraries make labels, so each must be read once: TILESPR.LIB reads TILELIB.LIB and SPRLIB.LIB, so include TILESPR.LIB alone; with CONST _FLOAT=1; GRAPH.LIB reads SOROBAN.LIB, so do not include SOROBAN.LIB as well. GRAPH.LIB and GRAPHF.LIB make the same labels, so include one of them.
In X1Pen, #INCLUDE and #CHAIN read the bundled include files, whatever the case of the name (#INCLUDE "graph.lib" finds GRAPH.LIB).
X1Pen sets ENV_TYPE to 1 and OS_TYPE to 0 and uses the x1 environment's default ORG of $0100.
#INCLUDE nesting is limited to 8 levels. #CHAIN filename continues with another file and does not return; anything after #CHAIN in the same file is not read.

#IF can use a CONST whose value is already known before it (its right-hand side may be an expression). A later CONST, a label, a FLOAT or an unknown name counts as 0, and a CONST declared inside a function cannot be used in #IF.

#INCLUDE looks next to the source and then in the bundle's include/ folder. X1Pen compiles only the program in the editor, so the eight bundled libraries GRAPH.LIB, GRAPHF.LIB, SOROBAN.LIB, CHIPLIB.LIB, SPRLIB.LIB, TILELIB.LIB, TILESPR.LIB and UILIB.LIB are the files that can be included.
slangc compiles #MODULE overlays into separate outputs, but X1Pen assembles and runs only the main program, so #MODULE is not usable in X1Pen.

title: PRINT formatting, strings and escapes
summary: PRINT accepts strings, numbers and formatting items. A slash emits a newline; string literals are zero-terminated addresses and support backslash escapes for X1 control codes, NUL and hexadecimal bytes.
syntax: "A\NB\0C"  // the bytes A, $0D, B, $00, C and the closing $00
notes: Common formatters include FORM$, DECI$, PN$, HEX2$, HEX4$, MSG$, MSX$, STR$, CHR$, SPC$, CR$, TAB$ and FL$.

The newline escape is backslash-N or backslash-slash and has value $0D. Backslash-C is clear-screen control $0C; backslash-R, -L, -U and -D are the cursor codes $1C, $1D, $1E and $1F; backslash-0 is $00; backslash-x followed by up to two hexadecimal digits is that byte; backslash before a backslash or quote gives that character. The escape letters may also be written in lower case.
Backslash-0 puts a $00 byte into the literal, and PRINT stops at the first $00: PRINT("A\NB\0C") prints A, a newline and B, while the C byte stays in memory after the NUL.
A FLOAT value cannot be printed directly; slangc reports A FLOAT value cannot be printed directly (use FL$(x)).

examples.title: Escapes, FL$ and hexadecimal output

title: System arrays, registers and core runtime functions
summary: SLANG exposes byte/word memory and port arrays, compatibility work arrays, Z80 register variables, and core helper routines supplied by the x1 runtime.
syntax: ABS(value) SGN(value) SEX(value) RND(limit) MIN(a,b) MAX(a,b)
notes: CALL and GETREG exchange values through registered Z80 register variables. ^CY is another name for ^CARRY.
@KBUFF is the address of the keyboard input buffer.
SOS and SOSW are compatibility work arrays provided by this compiler/runtime profile. Do not infer historical S-OS fixed-address layouts that are not documented by the runtime.

BIT, SET, RESET, ABS, SGN, SEX, RND, VTOS, GETREG and CALL are built-in functions with fixed argument counts that slangc checks (BIT, SET, RESET and VTOS 2; ABS, SGN, SEX, RND and CALL 1; GETREG 0). MEMCPY, MEMSET, STRLEN, MIN and MAX are runtime functions whose argument counts are not checked, so pass exactly the documented arguments.
MEM[], PORT[] and the other system arrays take one index.

title: X1Pen LSX line input and file runtime
summary: The x1 environment's LSX runtime provides line input and LSX file operations in addition to the core SLANG functions.
notes: File numbers are 0 through 7. FOPEN returns 255 for an invalid file number; otherwise it returns the LSX operation result.
FOPEN masks mode to two bits. Values below 3 open an existing file; mode 3 creates a file.
FSEEK origin is 0 from the beginning, 1 from the current position, or 2 from the end.

INPUT takes no arguments; GETL takes one; GETLIN and LINPUT take two. These are built-in functions and slangc rejects other counts. The file functions are runtime functions whose argument counts are not checked, so pass exactly the documented arguments. See the related INKEY entry for single-key polling and blocking modes.

examples.title: Open and close an LSX file

title: INKEY polling and blocking keyboard modes
summary: INKEY(mode) reads one X1 keyboard code: mode 0 polls current key state, mode 1 delegates one read to LSX DIRIN, and mode 2 or greater waits by polling until a key is nonzero.
notes: Mode 0 is non-blocking: it returns 0 when no key is pressed and polls current state, so a held key may be returned on consecutive calls. Use this mode in animation and game loops.

Mode 1 delegates each call to LSX DIRIN. A buffered input result can return immediately; with an empty buffer, the call waits for DIRIN input. One bounded host hold may reach no call, one call, or multiple following calls depending on guest speed, buffering, and key repeat, so this mode is not a one-physical-press edge guarantee. Programs that require one action per press must debounce or wait for release.
Every mode value 2 or greater blocks by repeatedly polling mode-0 state until nonzero. A held key may therefore satisfy consecutive calls.

In X1Pen's current default base X1 keyboard layout, Right/Left/Up/Down return $1C/$1D/$1E/$1F. F1 is mapped by its X1 physical position and returns lowercase q ($71). These are guest-layout results, not universal host key codes.
Alphabetic keys use the current guest modifier state; the unshifted A key returns lowercase a ($61). X1Pen maps host keys to JIS physical positions before the X1 keyboard table is read.

examples.title: Poll INKEY without stopping a frame loop

title: Defining X1 PCG characters with PCGDEF and PCGDEFS
summary: The x1 runtime defines one PCG glyph with PCGDEF or a consecutive range with PCGDEFS. Each 8x8 glyph is a 24-byte Blue/Red/Green interleaved bitmap. GETCGROM reads an ANK character's pattern from the CG ROM.
syntax: GETCGROM(code, address);  // 8 bytes, one per row
notes: Call WIDTH before PCGDEF/PCGDEFS because PCG setup depends on 40- or 80-column mode.
Pattern format is 8 rows x 3 bytes. Each row is Blue, Red, Green; bit 7 is the leftmost pixel.
PCGDEFS advances the source pointer by 24 and the character index by 1 for every glyph.
Hardware registration consumes one vertical blank per glyph, approximately count/60 seconds for PCGDEFS. Load assets during initialization, not every frame.
After registration the source pattern buffer can be reused. TILELIB map and index arrays, by contrast, remain referenced during drawing.
PCG indexes are 0 through 255 and share the text character-code space.
Defining a PCG pattern does not select it for display. Set attribute bit 5 on the target text cell with TATTR before printing the PCG character code.
WIDTH and other screen clears refill text attributes; issue TATTR again after a clear.

GETCGROM(code, address) writes the 8-byte pattern (one byte per row) of the ANK character code (the low byte) from the CG ROM to address. It reads in step with the display raster, so like PCGDEF it takes display time; it does not need a prior WIDTH call.
These are runtime functions: slangc does not check their argument counts, so pass exactly the documented arguments.

examples.title: Define and display a blue PCG glyph

title: Setting the current X1 text-cell attribute with TATTR
summary: TATTR(attribute) writes one attribute byte to the current LSX text cursor cell without changing its character code, kanji code or cursor position. It returns 1 on success and 0 when validation rejects the call.
notes: The argument is passed in HL as one SLANG word. Values 0000H through 00FFH are accepted; any nonzero high byte is rejected with HL=0 and no VRAM write. TATTR is a runtime function, so slangc does not check the argument count; pass exactly one.
On success HL returns 1. The low argument byte is written unchanged, so bits are 7=X2, 6=Y2, 5=PCG, 4=blink, 3=reverse and 2..0=BRG color.

The target is exactly the current LSX text cursor cell established by LOCATE or prior text output. TATTR takes no coordinates and does not move the cursor; a following PRINT writes at that same cell and then advances normally.

TATTR samples the cursor once and is not synchronized with an interrupt handler that relocates the text cursor. Do not depend on the sampled target while an ISR changes the cursor; ordinary LSX interrupt handlers do not do so.
The runtime writes the canonical attribute port 2000H plus the cursor offset with exactly one OUT. It does not write the 2800H mirror, ANK text VRAM or kanji VRAM and performs no input-port access.

Visible offsets are 0 through 999 in WIDTH(40) and 0 through 1999 in WIDTH(80). An offset outside the active range returns 0 with no write. LOCATE itself does not validate coordinates, so an invalid coordinate whose arithmetic aliases a visible offset is treated as that visible cell.
A program that calls neither WIDTH nor LOCATE uses LSX's initialized current cursor and the runtime's default 80-column width, so TATTR is still defined.
TATTR clobbers A, flags, BC and DE as allowed by the SLANG runtime calling convention. It preserves IX, IY, SP, the current text cursor and other persistent runtime work state.
TATTR executes no DI, EI or interrupt-mode operation; interrupt enable state is unchanged.
PRINT preserves an attribute already written to its target cell. WIDTH and other screen-clear paths refill or erase attributes, so issue TATTR again after a clear.
TATTR selects attributes only. PCGDEF or PCGDEFS must separately define a glyph pattern, and PRINT or another text writer must separately place its character code.

TATTR is part of the x1 environment's runtime (libx1_print.asm). PORT[$2000+offset]=attribute is the low-level equivalent, but then the caller must calculate and validate the current logical offset and keep the cursor contract itself.

examples.title: Select a white PCG glyph for the next printed cell

title: TILELIB, SPRLIB and TILESPR APIs
summary: X1Pen bundles a PCG tile-map library, a software-sprite library and a helper that synchronizes their double-buffer pages.
syntax: TILE_INIT() TILE_FILL_MAP() TILE_SET_MAP(3 args) TILE_SET_MAPSIZE(2 args)
TILE_SET_SCROLL(2 args) TILE_SET_ANIM(1 arg) TILE_SET_ANIM_RATE(2 args) TILE_ANIM_TICK()
TILE_SET_PAGE(1 arg) TILE_SET_OFS(2 args) TILE_SET_SIZE(2 args) TILE_INVALIDATE()
SPR_INIT() SPR_SET_PATTERN(2 args) SPR_SET_POS(3 args) SPR_SET_SHOW(2 args) SPR_IS_ACTIVE(1 arg) SPR_UPDATE()
notes: TILESPR.LIB includes TILELIB.LIB and SPRLIB.LIB itself. Include only TILESPR.LIB: slangc reads an #INCLUDE file every time it is named, so writing #INCLUDE "SPRLIB.LIB" or #INCLUDE "TILELIB.LIB" next to it puts that library in twice, and the program fails to assemble with Duplicate label errors. TILELIB.LIB (and so TILESPR.LIB) and CHIPLIB.LIB multiply with the runtime MULHLDE, asked for with ; @calls MULHLDE, so a program that includes them cannot have a function named MULHLDE (slangc stops with "; @calls MULHLDE: MULHLDE is a user function").
Initialize each subsystem before setting maps, patterns or positions. Call animation/update functions from the program's frame loop.
TILELIB uses 8x8 PCG glyphs as tiles. Four tile indexes in TL, TR, BL, BR order form one 16x16 super-chip; the map stores one super-chip number per byte.
Recommended setup order: WIDTH(40), PCGDEFS, TILE_INIT, TILE_SET_MAP, TILE_SET_MAPSIZE, optional animation setup, then TILE_FILL_MAP.
TILE_SET_MAP(map,index,0) keeps pointers to both arrays; keep them alive. Its third argument is reserved and must be 0.
TILE_SET_SCROLL uses character units (8 pixels). TILE_SET_MAPSIZE uses super-chip units. TILE_SET_SIZE uses character units and an even width is recommended.
For animation, reserve consecutive groups of up to four PCG indexes, set the threshold with TILE_SET_ANIM, call TILE_ANIM_TICK from VSYNC_PROC, and call TILE_FILL_MAP each frame.

The libraries declare their public calls with MACHINE and the parameter counts shown, so slangc rejects a call with a different number of arguments; consult the library source for argument meaning and memory layout.

title: CHIPLIB tile-chip and sprite APIs
summary: CHIPLIB exposes a compact tile-chip renderer, animation controls and a small sprite composition interface.
syntax: CHIP_SET_OFS(2 args) CHIP_SET_SIZE(2 args) CHIP_SET_MAP(3 args) CHIP_SET_MAPSIZE(2 args)
CHIP_SPR_START() CHIP_SPR_POS(2 args) CHIP_SPR_ADD(3 args) CHIP_SPR_FLASH(1 arg)
notes: Call CHIP_INIT before drawing. Configure offsets, sizes, map and VVRAM dimensions before the main draw loop.
For animation, call CHIP_ANIM_TICK from the program's VSYNC_PROC. A program that uses VSYNC must define that hook; an empty body is valid when no per-frame CHIP work is needed.
The public calls are MACHINE declarations with the counts shown, which slangc checks; use the bundled CHIPLIB.LIB comments and validation to confirm each argument's units.

The virtual-VRAM limits are CONST ASM values; a program can override them by defining CONST _CHIP_VVRAM_OVERRIDE = 1; and its own CONST ASM _CHIP_VVRAMW_MAX and _CHIP_VVRAMH_MAX before #INCLUDE CHIPLIB.LIB.

CHIPLIB.LIB multiplies with the runtime MULHLDE (asked for with ; @calls MULHLDE), so a program that includes it cannot have a function named MULHLDE, and a MULHLDE label or CONST ASM of its own fails to assemble with Duplicate label: MULHLDE. A multiplier written only so that CHIPLIB.LIB would build is no longer needed; remove it.

title: UILIB text UI API
aliases: ユーザーインターフェース
summary: UILIB provides cursor positioning and rasterized character/string drawing into graphics VRAM, plus color, fill and box operations for compact interfaces.
notes: UI_PUTS receives an address, normally a zero-terminated SLANG string literal or buffer.
The fill and box calls use compact packed arguments defined by UILIB; inspect its comments when constructing nontrivial layouts.
UI_SET_COLOR masks its argument to three bits and selects graphics-VRAM planes for UILIB's rasterizer. It does not write X1 text attribute VRAM; use TATTR for a hardware text cell attribute.

title: GRAPH and GRAPHF graphics libraries
summary: GRAPH provides the historical geometry package; GRAPHF is its version with native FLOAT and color variants for X1 graphics.
notes: GRAPH and GRAPHF are substantial packages with shared global buffers and compile-time feature switches; start from their headers and initialization routines rather than mixing calls blindly.
Prefer GRAPHF and native FLOAT for new X1Pen programs that need floating-point calculations.

GRAPHF.LIB replaces GRAPH.LIB rather than adding to it: both make the same labels, so include one of them only. With CONST _FLOAT=1; GRAPH.LIB includes SOROBAN.LIB itself, so do not include SOROBAN.LIB as well.
Some functions are conditional on constants in the include file. Validate the exact set used by the program.

title: Native 24-bit FLOAT runtime
summary: slangc has a native 24-bit FLOAT type, and the x1 runtime bundles conversion, trigonometric, logarithmic, power and random-number functions.
syntax: FSIN(x) FCOS(x) FTAN(x) FASIN(x) FACOS(x) FATAN(x)
notes: FLOAT values occupy three bytes. FLOAT functions return values in AHL.
Integers convert to FLOAT automatically where a typed FLOAT argument is expected. FLOAT-to-integer conversion is explicit through FTOI.

The runtime declares argument types for these functions: FTOI and the one-argument F functions take one FLOAT, FPOW(x,y) (x to the power y) and FLOGY(x,y) (logarithm of x to base y) take two FLOATs passed in AHL and CDE, and ITOF and UTOF take one integer. slangc checks their argument counts, converts an integer passed for a FLOAT, and rejects a FLOAT passed for an integer.

FLOAT values may be used in + - * / (also ./. and .*.), unary - and +, comparisons (which give integer 0/1), ?:, assignments, FLOAT ++ -- += -= *= /=, FLOAT parameters and return values, and as the single argument of a one-argument MACHINE. They are errors as a condition, in PRINT (use FL$), with MOD, AND, OR, XOR, CPL, shifts, signed comparisons, HIGH and LOW, as an index or address, and in FOR; convert with FTOI.

Constant FLOAT arithmetic is folded to the exact value where a FLOAT is needed (5.0 / 2.0 gives 2.5 when assigned to a FLOAT) and as an integer elsewhere (5.0 / 2.0 is 2 in a condition, an index, an integer target or a CONST). Values that 24-bit FLOAT cannot represent exactly, such as 1.0 / 3.0, are computed at run time.
Use the native FLOAT runtime for new X1Pen code. SOROBAN is primarily for compatibility with older sources.

examples.title: Calculate a square root with native FLOAT

title: X1 display and low-level graphics runtime
summary: The x1 runtime controls text width and cursor state, reads text-screen characters, and provides low-level line, XOR-line, paint and box-fill primitives.
notes: Call WIDTH before PCG setup and call GRPSETUP after selecting the intended 40/80-column mode; the line routines patch themselves for 320- or 640-dot width.
SCREEN(x,y) returns the character at the text-screen position. PRMODE is retained for source compatibility but is not supported by the LSX-Dodgers runtime and returns without changing mode.
GRDISP(0) hides graphics by setting the palette to 0; a nonzero argument selects the 8-color palette and bank 0 and shows graphics.
SET_PAINTBUF receives the start of a 1KB work buffer. BFILL requires x2>x1 and y2>y1.
WIDTH, LOCATE, SCREEN and PRMODE are built-in functions whose argument counts slangc checks; the graphics calls are runtime functions whose counts it does not check.
For higher-level geometry use GRAPH or GRAPHF; for game-oriented sprite rendering consider SGL or the tile libraries.

title: X1 PSG music and sound-effects runtime
summary: The X1 PSG driver plays three-channel BGM and priority-controlled sound effects, using either CTC-driven updates or explicit polling.
syntax: PSG_PROC();  // call periodically only in polling mode
notes: PSG_INIT(0) selects polling mode and requires regular PSG_PROC calls. A nonzero mode requests CTC operation and falls back to polling if CTC is unavailable.
BGM and SFX headers contain one tempo byte followed by three little-endian track addresses. Zero track addresses are allowed for SFX.
SFX playback compares the incoming priority byte with active BGM/SFX priorities before replacing channels.
Call PSG_END before abandoning an interrupt-driven driver so its CTC handler is restored.

The x1 runtime also contains ARKOS_* (Arkos Tracker AKG/AKM player) and BANJO_* (banjo player for Furnace songs) calls. They only jump into a player binary: the program defines its load address with CONST ASM ARKOS_BASE = ...; or CONST ASM BANJO_BASE = ...; and must load that player binary there at run time. X1Pen does not supply these player binaries.

examples.title: Initialize and stop the PSG polling driver

title: X1 joystick input with STICK
summary: STICK reads the raw active-low byte for X1 joystick port 1 or 2 through PSG register 14 or 15, and keeps the caller's interrupt state and PSG register 7.
notes: Only the exact word arguments 0 and 1 are valid. Every other value returns 255 ($00FF) at once, without selecting a PSG register or changing interrupt state.
The result is zero-extended to a SLANG word. Joystick bits are active-low: 0 means pressed, and 255 (FFH) means no direction or button is pressed.
The Web emulator combines JoyKey keyboard input, physical joystick input, and external Automation/MCP pad input before STICK reads the selected register.
For successive raw samples, (NEW XOR OLD) AND OLD yields the newly pressed bits. OLD=FFH and NEW=FEH produces 01H for a new Up press.

While it reads, STICK clears the port's bit in PSG register 7 (bit 6 for port A, bit 7 for port B) so the port is an input, and then writes register 7 back with its previous value. The read therefore works even after the PSG sound driver has made port B an output, and the mixer and sound state are left as they were.

STICK disables interrupts only while it uses the PSG, so a concurrent PSG sound update cannot change the selected register, and then restores the interrupt state it was called with: after the caller's DI it returns with interrupts still disabled, and with interrupts enabled it enables them again. It reads that state with LD A,I and checks for the NMOS Z80 case where an interrupt at that instruction hides an enabled state.
Do not call STICK from an interrupt handler, in particular an NMI handler: there the saved state reads as enabled and STICK would enable interrupts before RETN.
STICK is a runtime function: slangc does not check its argument count, so pass exactly one argument.
Buttons 3 and 4 are additional mappings exposed by the Web emulator; do not assume every physical two-button X1 controller drives those lines.

examples.title: Detect newly pressed joystick 1 bits

title: Vertical blank and CTC timing
summary: The X1 runtime exposes vertical-blank polling/wait helpers and CTC setup used by frame loops and time-based subsystems.
notes: VSYNC(frames) waits for that many counted vertical blanks and clears its internal counter afterward. It requires exactly one argument. slangc does not check the argument count of runtime functions, so VSYNC() still compiles but waits for whatever value happens to be in HL; always pass the frame count.

A program that links a vertical-blank path which references !VSYNC_PROC must define VSYNC_PROC(). This includes direct VSYNC use and SGL frame synchronization. The runtime calls the hook once for every counted frame; an empty body is valid. Without the hook the generated code jumps to an undefined VSYNC_PROC and assembly fails.
VSYNC1 waits directly for one vertical-blank transition.

X1_CTC_PORT() returns the CTC port that LSX-Dodgers detected, or 0 when there is none, and X1_CTC_VEC() returns the base of the interrupt vector table; programs pass them to ARKOS_SET_CTC_PORT or BANJO_SET_CTC_PORT to drive those players from the CTC.
TILE, CHIP and SGL libraries use the same !VSYNC_PROC hook; follow their documented update calls and setup order when composing frame work.

examples.title: Wait one frame with the required VSYNC hook

title: Compressed data and X1 image loaders
summary: The x1 runtime bundles LZE-family and ZX0 decompressors plus MAG and M8A image loaders for compact program assets.
notes: The decompressors operate on encoded byte streams and write directly to the destination address; allocate enough writable memory for the decoded result.

MAGLOAD uses LSX file operations and receives a filename address, X and Y. Choose it for an M8A-independent MAG file on mounted disk media; it is intended for 200-line X1 images and reserves substantial work buffers.
M8ALOAD receives the address of an M8A byte stream already in memory plus its X and Y graphics-VRAM origin. Keep the complete encoded data valid until the call returns; it performs no disk I/O.
M8ALOAD reads the current screen width from the X1 work area and links that area itself, so it can be the only X1 call of a program.

M8ALOAD writes the current X1 graphics VRAM but does not select or enable a visible graphics mode. For visible output, choose WIDTH(40) or WIDTH(80), initialize graphics for that layout, and enable graphics display before the call.
The compact example contains one 8-pixel group and one row. Its four $49 encoded pairs draw eight blue pixels at the graphics-VRAM origin.

examples.title: Draw an embedded M8A strip from memory

title: LSX-Dodgers X1 SGL sprite runtime
summary: The loaded libx1_sgl_lsx runtime provides pattern registration, sprite lifecycle and movement, page-flipped frame synchronization, and text rendering for LSX-Dodgers games.
notes: SGL_SPRCREATE returns zero on failure. Preserve nonzero handles and destroy sprites when they are no longer needed.
SGL_SPRDISP uses 0 for hidden and 1 for visible.
SGL_PRINT draws on the current render page; SGL_PRINT2 draws on both pages. SGL_VSYNC processes characters and flips the screen.
SGL frame synchronization invokes the program's VSYNC_PROC hook. Define the hook before using SGL frame waits; an empty body is valid when no additional per-frame work is needed.
The x1 environment loads libx1_sgl_lsx.asm, not the separate non-LSX libx1_sgl.asm that the SLANG-compiler runtime also contains.

title: SOROBAN compatibility numeric library
summary: SOROBAN.LIB supplies the older single/double numeric representation, conversion, comparison, arithmetic and transcendental routines used by historical SLANG sources.
notes: Prefer the compiler's native FLOAT type and libfloat functions for new X1Pen programs.
SOROBAN maintains its own numeric work representation and exposes many conditional routines. Read the include's switches before selecting functions.

title: X1Pen compiler and x1 (LSX-Dodgers) build profile
summary: X1Pen compiles SLANG with slangc 0.28.0 from the SLANG-compiler browser bundle at revision 3fb6f7f, in its x1 environment (ENV_TYPE=1, OS_TYPE=0, default ORG=$0100), assembles the generated Z80 source with its own assembler, then runs it under LSX-Dodgers.
notes: The x1 environment's runtime is runtime.asm, libfloat.asm, liblsx_base.asm, libx1_base.asm, libx1_grp.asm, liblsx_input.asm, libx1_print.asm, liblsx_file.asm, libx1_pcg.asm, libmag.asm, libm8a.asm, libx1_psg.asm, libcompress.asm, libsoroban.asm, libx1_magic.asm, libx1_sgl_lsx.asm, libx1_arkos.asm and libx1_banjo.asm. Only the routines a program calls, and the routines they depend on, are written into the output.
#INCLUDE files come from the bundle's include/ folder. The runtime depends on LSX-Dodgers 1.62c work addresses.

X1Pen assembles the generated source with ENV_TYPE=1 and OS_TYPE=0 defined. Compile errors and warnings are reported with line and column, and with the file name when the problem is in an included library.
The ASM editor content is generated output in SLANG mode. Edit the SLANG source, not the generated ASM.
x1pen_validate compiles SLANG and assembles its generated output without running it.
The MCP reference profile x1pen-slang-x1 is tied to compiler revision 3fb6f7fc17b54614e48e421a1a35e856c47a7ebc and is reviewed whenever X1Pen imports another bundle.

title: Compiler limits, diagnostics and common mistakes
summary: Keep array names attached to '[', remember that array bounds are inclusive, and stay within compiler nesting and storage limits. slangc reports a number of easy mistakes as errors.
syntax: ARRAY BYTE A[9];  // A[0] through A[9], ten elements
notes: Dynamic local area: 240 bytes per function. Parameters: at most 16 bytes per function (BYTE, WORD and arrays 2 bytes, FLOAT 3 bytes). Loop nesting: 16 levels.
Maximum source line length: 255 characters. Maximum name length: 32 characters. Include nesting: 8 levels.
FOR executes its body before checking the end condition.
FLOAT-to-integer conversion is not implicit; use FTOI.

Errors slangc reports that are easy to hit: a FLOAT as a condition (IF F THEN ...; compare with F <> 0.0 instead), PRINT of a FLOAT (use FL$), a side effect in the index of a ++/--/+=/-=/*=//= target (T[I++] += 1), using the value of a postfix ++/-- on a FLOAT, EXIT(n) with n not a constant from 1 to the number of enclosing loops, EXIT or CONTINUE outside a loop, a wrong argument count for a user function, MACHINE or built-in function, a function-local CONST that reuses a global name, and TRUE or FALSE as a variable name.
Runtime functions that are not declared to the compiler (VSYNC, STICK, TATTR and most other runtime calls) are not checked for argument count; a wrong count compiles and misbehaves at run time.

Some mistakes surface only when X1Pen assembles the output: a missing MAIN(), VSYNC without a VSYNC_PROC() function, or a library included twice (Duplicate label: SPRLIB.LIB or TILELIB.LIB next to TILESPR.LIB, which already reads them, or SOROBAN.LIB next to GRAPH.LIB with CONST _FLOAT=1;).
Validate frequently because included libraries consume memory and may impose initialization or buffer-address requirements not expressed by the language type system.
